title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: Vronsky had not even tried to sleep all that night. He sat in his armchair, looking straight before him or scanning the people getting in and out. If he had on previous occasions struck and impressed people who didn't know him with his air of unhesitating composure, he now seemed even more haughty and self-possessed than ever. He looked at people as though they were things. A nervous young man, a clerk in a law court sitting opposite him, hated him for that look. The young man asked him for a light and tried to start a conversation with him, even pushed against him, to make him feel that he was a person, not a thing. But Vronsky looked at him exactly as he did at the lamp, and the young man made a wry face, feeling that he was losing his composure under the oppression of this refusal to recognize him as a person.

Vronsky saw nothing and no one. He felt himself a king — not because he believed he had made an impression on Anna (he did not yet believe that), but because the impression she had made on him filled him with happiness and pride.

What would come of it all he did not know; he did not even think about it. He felt that all his powers, until now scattered and wasted, were now concentrated on one thing, and bent with fearful energy on one blissful goal. And he was happy at it. He knew only that he had told her the truth, that he had come where she was, that all the happiness of his life, the only meaning in life for him, now lay in seeing and hearing her. And when he got out of the carriage at Bologovo for some seltzer water, and caught sight of Anna, his first word had told her, in spite of himself, exactly what he was thinking. And he was glad he had told her, that she knew it now and was thinking about it. He did not sleep all night. Back in the carriage, he kept going over and over every attitude in which he had seen her, every word she had spoken, and before his fancy, making his heart faint with emotion, floated pictures of a possible future.

When he got out of the train at Petersburg, he felt, after his sleepless night, as keen and fresh as if he had just had a cold bath. He paused near his compartment, waiting for her to get out. "Once more," he said to himself, smiling without realizing it, "once more I shall see her walk, her face; she will say something, turn her head, glance, smile, perhaps." But before he caught sight of her, he saw her husband, whom the station-master was deferentially escorting through the crowd. "Ah, yes! The husband." Only now, for the first time, did Vronsky take in the fact that there was a person attached to her — a husband. He had known she had a husband, but he had hardly believed in his existence, and only now fully believed in him, with his head and shoulders and his legs in black trousers — especially when he saw this husband calmly take her arm with a sense of property.

Seeing Alexey Alexandrovitch with his Petersburg face and severely self-confident figure, in his round hat with his rather prominent back, he believed in him, and felt an unpleasant sensation — the kind a man tortured by thirst might feel on reaching a spring and finding a dog, a sheep, or a pig that had drunk from it and muddied the water. Alexey Alexandrovitch's walk, with its swing of the hips and flat feet, particularly annoyed Vronsky. He could recognize in no one but himself an unquestionable right to love her. But she was still the same, and the sight of her affected him the same way, physically reviving him, stirring him, and filling his soul with rapture. He told his German valet, who ran up to him from the second class, to take his things and go on, while he himself went up to her. He saw the first meeting between husband and wife, and noted with a lover's sharpness the signs of slight reserve with which she spoke to her husband. "No, she does not love him and cannot love him," he decided to himself.
Just as he was approaching Anna Arkadyevna, he noticed with joy too that she was aware of his being near, and looked round, and seeing him, turned back to her husband.

"Did you have a good night?" he asked, bowing to her and to her husband together, and leaving it for Alexey Alexandrovitch to take the bow as meant for him too, and to acknowledge it or not, as he saw fit.
"Thank you, very good," she answered.

Her face looked tired, and there was none of that play of eagerness in it, peeping out from her smile and her eyes; but for a single instant, as she glanced at him, there was a flash of something in her eyes, and although the flash died away at once, he was happy for that moment. She glanced at her husband to see whether he knew Vronsky. Alexey Alexandrovitch looked at Vronsky with displeasure, vaguely recalling who he was. Vronsky's composure and self-confidence struck, like a scythe against a stone, the cold self-confidence of Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"Count Vronsky," said Anna.
"Ah! We're acquainted, I believe," Alexey Alexandrovitch said indifferently, holding out his hand.
"You set off with the mother and come back with the son," he said, articulating each syllable as though each one were a separate favor he was conferring.
"You're back from leave, I take it?" he said, and without waiting for an answer turned to his wife in his bantering tone: "Were a great many tears shed in Moscow at parting?"
By addressing his wife this way, he let Vronsky know that he wished to be left alone, and, turning slightly toward him, he touched his hat; but Vronsky turned to Anna Arkadyevna.
"I hope I may have the honor of calling on you," he said.
Alexey Alexandrovitch glanced with his weary eyes at Vronsky.

"Delighted," he said coolly. "Mondays we're at home. Most fortunate," he said to his wife, dismissing Vronsky entirely, "that I should have just half an hour to meet you, so I could prove my devotion," he continued in the same bantering tone.

"You put too much emphasis on your devotion for me to value it much," she replied in the same jesting tone, listening in spite of herself to the sound of Vronsky's steps behind them. "But what does it have to do with me?" she said to herself, and she began asking her husband how Seryozha had got on without her.

"Oh, splendidly! Mariette says he has been very good. And... I must disappoint you... but he hasn't missed you as your husband has. But once again _merci,_ my dear, for giving me a day. Our dear _Samovar_ will be delighted." (He used to call Countess Lidia Ivanovna, well known in society, the samovar, because she was always bubbling over with excitement.) "She has been continually asking after you. And, do you know, if I may venture to advise you, you should go see her today. You know how she takes everything to heart. Just now, with all her own cares, she's worried about getting the Oblonskys back together."
Countess Lidia Ivanovna was a friend of her husband's, and the center of one of those coteries of the Petersburg world that Anna was, through her husband, most closely connected with.
"But you know I wrote to her?"

"Still she'll want to hear the details. Go and see her, if you're not too tired, my dear. Well, Kondraty will take you in the carriage, while I go to my committee. I shan't be alone at dinner again," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on, no longer in a sarcastic tone. "You wouldn't believe how I've missed..." And, with a long pressure of her hand and a meaningful smile, he put her into her carriage.
